title: refuses a patches/ffmpeg/.patches that lists a patch the pins do not hold
why: A patch Electron applies to FFmpeg that the pins do not hold: the source archive would lack a change to the shipped library.

title: refuses a pinned patches/ffmpeg patch that the list does not name
why: A pinned FFmpeg patch Electron no longer applies: the archive would offer a change the library does not carry.

title: reads a listed name that begins with a dash as a name, not a grep option
why: A listed name read as a grep option: a name made to match another's pattern passes as pinned, so the archive lacks a patch the list names.

title: matches a patches/ffmpeg/.patches with CRLF line ends in both directions
why: A list with CRLF line ends no name of which matches a pinned one: every cached archive built from it is refused, or its names are never compared.

title: refuses an archive with no patches/ffmpeg/.patches, naming it
why: A missing list read as an empty one: the pinned patches would then be refused for not being listed, or none checked at all.

title: checks the list of FFmpeg patches in the fetch and in --verify
why: --verify without the list check: a cached archive missing a patch the library carries verifies and is attached to a release.

title: opens every case pattern inside a $( ... ) with "("
why: A bare case pattern inside $( ... ) is a syntax error to macOS's bash 3.2, so every --verify on a Mac runner exits 2. Read from the text, so the mutation goes red on Linux too, where bash 5 would parse it.

title: finds a bare pattern on the case line and on the lines after it, and nothing else
why: A here-document's text read as the shell's: a line of Python that happens to say "case x in y)" would be called a bare pattern.

title: finds a bare pattern on the case line and on the lines after it, and nothing else
why: Every line of a case body taken for a pattern: a command holding a $( ... ) would be called a bare pattern and fail a legal script.

title: finds a bare pattern on the case line and on the lines after it, and nothing else
why: A case on the same line as its $( unread, so its bare pattern goes unseen.

title: refuses an archive that does not unpack, by that name
why: A tar that refuses the archive read as having unpacked: a damaged archive goes on to the later checks and is refused, if at all, for some other reason.

title: refuses an archive that does not unpack, by that name
why: The unpack's own status dropped: the sentence that names the archive as unreadable is never said.

title: checks the list of FFmpeg patches in the fetch and in --verify
why: The pins' word where an archive is being judged: --verify's refusal would speak of the pins, when what it was given is an archive, and the fetch's would speak of an archive where none exists yet.

find:
archive) fail "the archive lacks patches/ffmpeg/.patches, which says which patches Electron applies to FFmpeg" ;;
    pins) fail "the pins do not hold patches/ffmpeg/.patches, which says which patches Electron applies to FFmpeg: add it to electron_files" ;;
replace:
archive) fail "the pins do not hold patches/ffmpeg/.patches, which says which patches Electron applies to FFmpeg: add it to electron_files" ;;
    pins) fail "the archive lacks patches/ffmpeg/.patches, which says which patches Electron applies to FFmpeg" ;;
title: words it for the archive under archive) and for the pins under pins)
why: The two sentences under each other's word: the fetch would say an archive lacks the list where none exists yet, and --verify would say the pins do not hold it when it is judging an archive.

find: *) fail "check_patch_list was called without saying whether it judges the archive or the pins" ;;
title: refuses a call that does not say what it judges, rather than choose a wording
why: A third call site that names no word would fall through the case with no refusal, and a missing list would pass.
